# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book is a hands-on tutorial on two questions that come up in almost
every RNA-seq project:

1. **Which genes change in expression** between two conditions?
   (differential expression, DE)
2. **Which transcripts are spliced differently**, including splicing events
   that are missing from the reference annotation?
   (alternative and cryptic splicing)

We answer both questions with one public data set, from the first download
to the sentence you would write in the Methods section. Every number in the
book comes from code that you can run yourself.

## The running example

TDP-43 (gene *TARDBP*) is an RNA-binding protein. It is the main component of
the protein inclusions found in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and in the
most common pathological form of frontotemporal lobar degeneration
[@neumann2006], and neurons that carry these inclusions often lose TDP-43
from the nucleus. One of its nuclear jobs is to keep "cryptic" exons out of
mature mRNA. These are stretches of intron that
look enough like exons to be spliced in when TDP-43 is not there to repress
them [@ling2015]. When TDP-43 is depleted, cryptic exons appear in transcripts
such as *STMN2* and *UNC13A*
[@klim2019; @melamed2019; @brown2022; @ma2022].

This makes TDP-43 knockdown a very good teaching case:

- the expected direction of change is known (cryptic exons go **up** when
  TDP-43 goes **down**), so we can check our methods against a positive
  control;
- cryptic exons are, by definition, **not in the annotation**, so they show
  why annotation-based tools are not enough on their own;
- the effect on gene expression (for example lower *STMN2*) and the splicing
  change that causes it can be studied in the same samples.

We use the study by @klim2019, who knocked down TDP-43 with siRNA in motor
neurons derived from the human embryonic stem cell line HUES3. The data are
SRA study **SRP166282** (GEO series GSE121569). They are part of
**recount3** [@wilks2021], which has already aligned every sample to GRCh38
and summarised it with GENCODE release 26. So we do not need to align a
single read for the main analysis.

## Analysis standards used throughout

These rules are applied in every chapter and explained where they first
appear. They are fixed **before** looking at any result.

- One genome (GRCh38) and one annotation (GENCODE v26) for everything.
  We never mix Ensembl and GENCODE releases in one project.
- DE: control is set as the reference level explicitly, genes need at least
  10 counts in at least as many samples as the smallest group, and we report
  raw and apeglm-shrunken log2 fold changes in separate columns.
- Thresholds: padj < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1 for DE; FDR < 0.05 and
  |ΔPSI| > 0.1 for splicing. Thresholds are never adjusted to the result.
- Volcano plots use padj, heatmaps use variance-stabilised values with row
  z-scores, and GSEA always states its ranking metric.
- Strandedness is measured, not assumed.
- A cryptic exon claim needs junction read counts **and** a visual check.
- RNA-seq on its own does not show a change in protein or function. A
  consistent trend that does not pass FDR is an *exploratory signal*, not a
  finding.

## How to read this book

Each chapter starts with the question it answers, works through the code,
and ends with a short **Check your understanding** box. The code is meant to
be run in order, but every chapter can also be rendered on its own: shared
helper functions live in `R/helpers.R`, and downloads are cached in
`data-cache/`.

The source is at
<https://github.com/elmasnuryilmaz/rnaseq-splicing-tutorial>. Corrections
and questions are welcome as GitHub issues.

::: {.callout-note}
## Who this is for
You should be comfortable with basic R (data frames, functions, `ggplot2`)
and with the biology of transcription and splicing. You do not need prior
experience with Bioconductor.
:::
